core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes conservative care (activity modification, NSAIDs, physical therapy) for 4-6 weeks before considering imaging or injection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp electric pain radiating down back of leg to ankle with numbness and positive straight leg raise after lifting heavy box

Key HPI features: 38M warehouse worker presenting with acute onset of sharp, electric pain radiating from his low back down the posterior leg to the ankle, with associated numbness, since lifting a heavy box at work 3 days ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Antalgic gait, lumbar paraspinal tenderness and spasm, reduced lumbar flexion due to pain. Positive straight leg raise on the affected side reproducing radicular leg pain below the knee. Diminished ankle reflex (S1) and decreased sensation over the lateral foot/sole, with mildly reduced plantarflexion strength. No saddle anesthesia, normal rectal tone, no bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lumbar Radiculopathy (Sciatica).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Lumbar spinal stenosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence).
management_principles: Screen thoroughly for cauda equina red flags (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction, bilateral symptoms) at presentation and at every follow-up
First-line treatment is conservative: activity modification, NSAIDs, and structured physical therapy (e.g., McKenzie exercises), typically for 4-6 weeks before escalation
Reserve MRI for red-flag features, progressive or significant motor deficit, or failure to improve after 6 weeks of conservative care
Escalate to epidural steroid injection or surgical referral if conservative management fails or a significant motor deficit develops.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 38M warehouse worker presenting with acute onset of sharp, electric pain radiating from his low back down the posterior leg to the ankle, with associated numbness, since lifting a heavy box at work 3 days ago.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Antalgic gait, lumbar paraspinal tenderness and spasm, reduced lumbar flexion due to pain. Positive straight leg raise on the affected side reproducing radicular leg pain below the knee. Diminished ankle reflex (S1) and decreased sensation over the lateral foot/sole, with mildly reduced plantarflexion strength. No saddle anesthesia, normal rectal tone, no bowel/bladder dysfunction.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute L5/S1 lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica), most consistent with disc herniation, without cauda equina red flags.
reference_soap.plan: Begin conservative management: activity modification, NSAIDs, and a structured physical therapy program (e.g., McKenzie-directional exercises) with reassessment in 4-6 weeks. Reserve MRI for red-flag features, progressive neurologic deficit, or failure to improve after 6 weeks of conservative care. Refer for epidural steroid injection or surgical evaluation if conservative treatment fails or a significant motor deficit develops, and educate the patient on cauda equina warning signs requiring immediate return.

teaching.one_liner: Compression or inflammation of a lumbar nerve root causing sharp radiating leg pain, numbness, and motor weakness.
red_flags: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence)

must_ask.say: Does the pain shoot down past your knee into your foot or toes?
Does coughing, sneezing, or sitting down make the leg pain much worse?
Have you noticed any numbness around your buttocks or loss of bowel or bladder control?
Does raising your straight leg while lying flat trigger the shooting pain?
Do you feel weakness when walking on your heels or toes?
